(Family Letter No. 3)
Tokyo
January 26, 1950
Dear Family,
I left Bangkok on the morning of the 21st, arriving
Hongkong that afternoon.
Won't attempt to report on Siam as
I'm sure Debby and Hebe will write fully. I did accept an
invitation to go to a Siamese-style prizefight from which I
managed - with some difficulty - to extricate Debby and Hebe,
only to learn by letter from Debby that Hebe accepted an in-
vitation from one of her boyfriends to go to a worse one on
the Sunday after I left. The fights are prefaced by each con-
testant bowing in prayer; then he goes through a pantomime
routine to show the fans whet he is going to do to his opponent -
and how.
The fighters wear gloves but no shoes, and anything
goes except biting in the clinches, if they get
caught at it!
They kick - either above or below the waist - use their knees,
butt with their heads and flay their opponent with their elbows.
The pace is terrific and knockouts numerous.
I know you'll want to hear about poor old CNAC. I haven't
written earlier because I didn't know the whole story myself
until I talked to Bond at Hongkong.
When Bond and I returned to New York in December we
first got a fix from PAA as to what course we might pursue, then
went to flashington to talk to the State Department.
Our American
staff in CNAC had agreed unanimously that they would not go along
with the new regime in China unless and until such cooperstion
was approved by our State Department. Furthermore, we knew that
the British were soon going to recognize the Red government of
China.
Therefore, we were faced with the necessity of knowing
whet our Government wanted us to do if a new Managing Director
welked into Hongkong and started giving orders as the represen-
tative of the Chinese Reds.
We asked the question, "Shall we
go along or not?
If not, as PAA how about the American staff?
Do you want such of them
as are willing to join the new regime
or do you want them to refuse to cooperate?
We must know and
we have a right to expect an answer."
The officials to whom we
talked agreed that we were entitled to an answer but said - in
State Department ianguage - that it wes a very hot potato.
They
would try to give us an answer within a few days, and Bond would
stand by in Washington to get said answer.
That was on Thursday,
December 15th.
December 19th, the Department advised Bond that they did not
want us to go along with the Chinese Communists, nor did they
want Americans to offer technical or advisory assistance. About
the same time Bond heard that the National Government of Chiang
Kai-shek had sold its 80% interest in CNAC to General Chennault.
Bond immediately got in touch with his friend, I.V. Soong, and
made a deal to sell our 20% to the National Government for

-2.
$1,250,000 cash with no strings attached. It was, of course,
in view of the State Department's stand, the one course left
open to us.
Bond made a wonderful deal under all the cir-
cumstances and PAA got the money on December 30th.
At Hongkong the British refused to recognize the sale
even though it was made by
the then British-recognized gov-
ernment of China and covered
property which was legally theirs
to dispose of as they wished.
The whole question of title to
the aircraft is now before the Hongkong court. Meanwhile, the
British have recognized the Communist government.
The airport
is covered with airplanes and the only flying is being done by
swarms of buzzard-like lawyers waiting to swoop down on any
claim which appears vulnerable.
I stayed in Hongkong only two days and then came up
here after making arrangements for Debby and Hebe to get hotel
space from February 10th to 16th in the Colony. We felt they
should leave Bangkok before the big meeting of diplomats which
will be held there starting February 13th as hotel accommodations
in Bangkok are both scarce and sub-standard.
Having spent a few deys in India enroute here I feel
as well qualified as most experts to discuss the India-Pakistan
You know what was formeriy India, a piece of pie-
shaped land, is now divided very roughly by a wide strip down
from the broad top to either side of the point, and that section
is called India.
It takes in Calcutta on the east and Bombay
on the west but does not include Karadhi which is the capital
of Pakistan.
The small sections on either side of this wide
strip are called East Pakistan and West Pakistan.
The citizens
of the latter country are Moslems while the Indians are Hindus.
Such is the hatred of the one for the other that there can be
no peace between them.
Both claimed the erstwhile independent
Hyderabad, the ruler of which wes Moslem but the big majority
of the people were Hindus; Pandit Nehru took Hyderabad by force
of arms but he contends with respect to the only large inde-
pendent state left (i.e. Kashinir) that India must have that,
too although the situation in Kashmir is exactly the reverse
of Hyderabad only in this instance the ruler of Kashmir is a
Hindu and the people are probably 80% Moslem.
Apparently
among politicians - no matter how elevated their speeches -
consistency is not a virtue.
The pity of the whole thing is that both countries
are spending the largest part of their national income on war
meterial
and military establishments. Another tragic con-
sequence is that Pakistan is more than self-sufficient on food-
stuff while thousands of Indiens are starving. Nevertheless,
Pakistan is exporting wheat to Europe while its neighbor
India is importing wheat from Australia.
Furthermore, Pakistan
has large dollar receipts from the sale of long staple cotton,
wheat, hides, jute and minerals while India must import many
of these products in order to run its industriel plants, but
Pakistan won't sell to them. India has a population of

-3-
300,000,000 while Pakistan has 80,000,000, but a Pakistan
official with whom we traveled said that all the really good
soldiers in World Wars I as well as II came from Pakistan,
and that in the
event of war between the two countries
Pakistan would win despite the greater number of Indians.
From what I have seen of the latter I would be inclined to
agree with him.
The Kashmir dispute may be settled by a
plebiscite conducted by the U.N. but so far Nehru has been
unwilling to abide by any such procedure because he knows
that
in an honest election India would lose.
But unless that
question is settled soon there may be an outbreak of war
between the tro countries.
I hope the foregoing hasn't bored you. I knew so
little about the countries and problems and all explanations
have been so complicated that I
thought you might be interested
in a brief - perhaps over-simplified - description.
If I can finish my work here in time will fly back
to Honkong to join Debby and Hebe. If not I will join them
here at Tokyo on February 17th and go on with them to Midway
and Honolulu.
Incidentally, because of the dateline of course,
the scheduled time of arrival in Honolulu is two hours earlier
than the departure time from Tokyo.
This plan is slightly different than our original
itinerary but we hope to travel westward from Honolulu through
Wake, Guam, Manila to Singapore and Batavia. Bond left Hongkong
the day after I did
for Menila where he was to meet George
McClelland (whose sister married Bill Barrett's brother) and
go on to Batavia for talks about the extension of PAA service
from Singapore to Batavia.
If they are successful we may be
able to fly PAA all the way.
As ever,
H. M. B.

Soong.
